subChunks.title: Science Policy & Government
subChunks.hookHtml:
'Vannevar Bush wrote a report in 1945,' Theodora said, setting a photocopied document on the table. 'Science — The Endless Frontier. Written for President Roosevelt, finished after his death and delivered to Truman. Its argument was simple and enormously consequential: basic research is the seed corn of applied science and technology; government should fund it generously without directing it; and universities should be the primary vehicle. That report shaped US science policy for decades. The NSF, NIH, DARPA — all its children.'

'The irony is that the linear model Bush assumed — basic research flows naturally into applied science flows naturally into technology — has been substantially disproven by historians and sociologists of innovation. Most major technologies emerged from a more tangled process: applied needs driving basic research, accidents converted to products by alert entrepreneurs, government and industry and universities interlocked in ways the linear model cannot capture. But the model endured in policy because it justified generous science funding in terms politicians could sell to taxpayers.'

She folded the document away. 'Science policy is the set of decisions that determine what science gets done, by whom, with what resources, and in service of what goals. It is irreducibly political. The scientist who says she does not engage in science policy is simply ceding that ground to others who will engage on her behalf — or against her.'
subChunks.explanationHtml:
What Science Policy Is

Science policy encompasses: research funding decisions (what topics, at what levels, through which mechanisms); governance of scientific institutions (universities, national laboratories, research councils); regulation of scientific activities (clinical trials, biosafety, data privacy); use of scientific evidence in policy-making; international scientific cooperation; and intellectual property regimes. It operates at national, international, and supranational levels.

The major national science funding structures: in the US, the National Science Foundation (NSF, ~$9B/year), National Institutes of Health (NIH, ~$47B/year), Department of Energy Office of Science, and DARPA; in the UK, UKRI (umbrella for seven research councils, ~£8B/year), Wellcome Trust; in the EU, Horizon Europe (~€95.5B over 2021–2027). These agencies shape what science is done through funding mechanisms, priority areas, grant review processes, and overhead policies.

Models of the Science-Policy Relationship

The linear model (Bush 1945): basic research → applied research → development → commercialisation → societal benefit. Criticised as historically inaccurate (most technologies did not emerge through this sequence) and normatively misleading (it implies basic science needs no justification beyond its potential eventual applicability).

Pasteur's quadrant (Stokes 1997): a two-dimensional taxonomy of research by use-inspiration and quest for fundamental understanding. Pure basic research (Bohr's atom); pure applied research (Edison's incremental improvements); use-inspired basic research (Pasteur, whose germ theory work was simultaneously theoretically fundamental and practically motivated). Stokes argues science policy should fund all quadrants, not privilege the pure basic research framing of the Bush model.

Mode 2 knowledge production (Gibbons et al. 1994): argues that science increasingly operates in an application context (not just academic discipline contexts), is transdisciplinary, socially accountable, and quality-controlled by relevance as well as peer review. Mode 1 (traditional disciplinary, curiosity-driven, peer-reviewed) coexists with Mode 2 (problem-driven, interdisciplinary, heterogeneous team-based, societal accountability). Mode 2 is controversial — critics argue it undermines the autonomy of science; advocates argue it describes a real and legitimate shift in knowledge production.

Evidence-Based Policy and Its Limits

Evidence-based policy (EBP) is the aspiration that policy decisions are informed by the best available evidence, evaluated rigorously (preferably via systematic review and meta-analysis). The UK's Government Social Research, the US Congressional Budget Office, and WHO guideline development processes exemplify institutional EBP. The evidence hierarchy privileges RCTs and systematic reviews.

EBP faces persistent challenges: (1) the evidence base is often thin, contested, or irrelevant to the policy question being asked; (2) policy operates under time pressure and uncertainty incompatible with waiting for definitive evidence; (3) evidence answers 'what works?' but not 'for whom, under what conditions, at what cost?'; (4) policy involves values (distributional equity, liberty, fairness) that evidence cannot adjudicate; (5) powerful interests systematically produce and suppress evidence to advance their agendas (tobacco industry, fossil fuel companies, pharmaceutical companies). The precautionary principle — in the absence of certainty, act to prevent serious harm — is the alternative epistemic approach for high-stakes, irreversible decisions.

Scientific Advice to Government

Most governments maintain a chief scientific adviser or equivalent: the UK Government Chief Scientific Adviser (GCSA), the US President's Council of Advisors on Science and Technology (PCAST), the EU Chief Scientific Adviser (discontinued 2014, replaced by Science Advice for Policy by European Academies, SAPEA). During crises — pandemic, nuclear accident, climate extremes — scientific advisory structures are stress-tested: SAGE in the UK during COVID-19, the CDC and NIAID in the US.

The COVID-19 pandemic revealed structural tensions: SAGE's advice (modelling-based) was sometimes at odds with NERVTAG's (clinical), PHE's (epidemiological), and economic advisers' views. The phrase 'following the science' was both politically useful and scientifically misleading — science provided models with wide uncertainty intervals; policy required specific decisions about timing, thresholds, and trade-offs that science alone could not specify. The 'sage science' was systematically filtered through ministerial and communications preferences before reaching the public.

International Science Governance

Science operates globally but is governed nationally. Major international science governance bodies: the Intergovernmental Panel on Climate Change (IPCC, assessment not research), the International Energy Agency, the Biosafety Protocol (Cartagena), CERN (particle physics), ITER (fusion), ISS (space station), and science provisions in trade agreements (TRIPS, intellectual property). Open science — the movement for open data, open access publication, open code — is both a scientific and a governance issue, reshaping incentives in the research economy.

storyBeats.text: 'Pasteur's quadrant is the most useful reframing of science policy in the last thirty years. Not: basic versus applied. But: fundamental understanding versus use-inspiration. Pasteur's germ theory was both profoundly theoretical and directly aimed at preventing disease. That is where the most important science often lives — in the quadrant that serves both goals simultaneously.'

'The precautionary principle is genuinely difficult. Interpreted too weakly, it has no teeth — every policy can claim precaution. Interpreted too strongly, it paralyses action, because any action has uncertain consequences. The most defensible version: where there is credible evidence of serious and irreversible harm, the burden of proof shifts to those proposing the action, not those opposing it.'

'SAGE during COVID: a committee of eighty-plus experts generating probabilistic model outputs with enormous uncertainty bands. Ministers needed a single number — a tier threshold, a school closure date. The translation was necessarily lossy. The 'following the science' rhetoric obscured that value judgements about acceptable risk were being made constantly, just without public scrutiny.'

'Tobacco companies spent decades and millions funding research that raised doubt about the causal link between smoking and cancer. Not to prove smoking was safe — they could not — but to maintain the appearance of scientific controversy where there was scientific consensus. The manufactured uncertainty strategy has been used since by fossil fuel interests, pesticide manufacturers, and pharmaceutical companies. Understanding it is a form of scientific literacy.'

'Open science is a governance choice with distributional consequences. Open access publication shifts costs from journal subscriptions to article processing charges — expensive for small institutions in developing countries. Open data assumes sufficient computing and analytic resources to use the data. Equity-unaware open science can widen rather than close the gap between resource-rich and resource-poor research communities.'

subChunks.feynmanPrompt: Explain to a 16-year-old what the precautionary principle is and give one example where you think it should be applied and one where applying it too strictly would cause problems.
learningObjectives: Evaluate the linear model of innovation and Pasteur's quadrant as frameworks for understanding the science-policy relationship
Explain evidence-based policy and its limitations, including the role of values and the problem of manufactured uncertainty
Analyse the structure and limitations of scientific advisory systems, using COVID-19 SAGE as a case study
Assess the equity implications of open science initiatives for global research participation
commonMistakes: Treating 'following the science' as a complete description of evidence-based policy — scientific evidence constrains policy options but does not determine which option to choose among those consistent with the evidence
Applying the precautionary principle without specifying its conditions — both the risks of action and inaction require evidence-based assessment
Conflating Pasteur's quadrant with a simple 'basic vs applied' dichotomy — the two-dimensional framework is specifically designed to reject this conflation
Assuming open science is uniformly beneficial without examining who bears the costs and who gains access under different open science models
assessmentCriteria: Accurately explains Stokes's Pasteur quadrant model and applies it to a concrete research example, distinguishing it from the linear model
Critically evaluates the role of scientific advisory committees during a crisis, identifying where science ended and value judgement began
Identifies and analyses at least two strategies used by industrial actors to manufacture scientific uncertainty, with historical examples
Evaluates an open science policy proposal for equity implications, identifying who benefits and who bears costs
subChunks.guidedPracticeHtml:
Case Study: IPCC and Climate Policy

The Intergovernmental Panel on Climate Change (IPCC) is an international scientific body that assesses climate change research — it does not conduct original research, but synthesises existing literature. Its Assessment Reports (now in their sixth cycle) are written by hundreds of scientists and reviewed by governments, then approved line-by-line by governmental representatives. They are explicitly designed to be 'policy-relevant but not policy-prescriptive'.

  1. Apply Stokes's Pasteur quadrant: where does IPCC Assessment Report work fall, and why? Is it Mode 1 or Mode 2 knowledge production?
  2. The IPCC's Summary for Policymakers (SPM) is approved by government representatives who can request changes to wording. Evaluate: does this process strengthen or weaken the authority of the IPCC's scientific findings?
  3. Some IPCC Working Group III (mitigation) findings are routinely more contested than Working Group I (physical science) findings. Why? What does this reveal about the science-policy interface?
  4. Apply Pielke's honest broker concept: what role does the IPCC play, and is this the appropriate role for an intergovernmental scientific body?
subChunks.guidedPracticeModelAnswer:
1. Pasteur's quadrant: IPCC Assessment Report work sits primarily in use-inspired basic research (Pasteur's quadrant) — it synthesises science driven by both the quest for understanding climate dynamics and the practical goal of informing climate policy. It is more Mode 2 than Mode 1: transdisciplinary (physical science, economics, sociology, engineering), conducted in an application context (policy relevance is an explicit design goal), accountable to a diverse set of stakeholders (governments, civil society, industry), and quality-controlled by policy relevance as well as scientific rigour. The SPM approval process introduces a governance dimension not present in Mode 1 knowledge production.

2. Government approval of the SPM: The line-by-line governmental approval process is both a strength and a weakness. Strength: it ensures that governments feel ownership of and cannot disown the summary, increasing its policy legitimacy. Weakness: governments (particularly oil-producing states) have used the approval process to weaken or delay language that reflects the underlying scientific consensus — there is documented tension between scientists' drafted text and government-approved SPM language. The process does not change the underlying scientific assessment but may create a gap between what the science says and what the approved summary asserts. Overall, it is a legitimacy-securing mechanism with a cost in scientific fidelity.

3. WG I vs WG III: WG I (physical climate science) produces findings with strong empirical grounding — temperature records, ice cores, atmospheric measurements — that are scientifically mature and largely non-controversial within the scientific community. WG III (mitigation) involves assessment of economic, social, and political dimensions of emissions reduction — areas where values, distributional questions, and economic modelling assumptions play central roles. Disagreements in WG III often reflect genuine value differences (who should bear the cost of mitigation?) rather than factual uncertainties. This reveals that the science-policy distinction dissolves in WG III: the 'science' of mitigation is shot through with normative assumptions that scientific expertise alone cannot adjudicate.

4. Honest broker: The IPCC is explicitly designed as an honest broker — 'policy-relevant but not policy-prescriptive'. It presents the range of scenarios, pathways, and their consequences without advocating for a specific policy. In practice, this is difficult to sustain: the framing of 1.5°C as a target threshold (from the Paris Agreement, which IPCC then assessed) creates a de facto policy advocacy frame. The IPCC's 'code red for humanity' rhetoric in 2021 (from the WMO Secretary-General, not the IPCC itself) illustrates how the institutional context blurs the honest broker/advocate distinction. The IPCC is the closest institutional approximation to an honest broker at the international level, but the complexity of the science-policy boundary means it inevitably drifts toward advocacy at times.
subChunks.soloPracticeHtml: Write a 350-word policy brief addressed to a fictional government minister, advising on whether to approve the use of CRISPR gene editing in agricultural crops (specifically, drought-resistant wheat). Your brief should: (a) distinguish what the scientific evidence says from what it does not determine; (b) identify the key value judgements that the government must make; (c) apply the precautionary principle appropriately; and (d) recommend a governance mechanism (regulatory approval process, public consultation, sunset clause, etc.) justified by your analysis.
subChunks.modelAnswer:
Policy Brief: Gene-Edited Wheat — Decision Framework for Minister

(a) What the evidence says: CRISPR gene editing of wheat to improve drought tolerance is technically feasible and has been demonstrated in field trials. Unlike transgenic GM crops, CRISPR edits can produce changes indistinguishable from those arising through conventional breeding (small deletions or modifications within the existing genome). Current evidence finds no novel safety risks from precisely gene-edited crops relative to conventionally bred varieties. The scientific consensus (NASEM 2016, EFSA 2020) is that risk assessment should focus on the trait introduced, not the technique used.

What the evidence does not determine: (i) long-term ecological effects on soil microbiomes, pollinators, and weed dynamics; (ii) socioeconomic effects on small farmers if large agribusinesses own the patents; (iii) whether drought-resistant varieties will actually reach farmers in low-income countries, where drought risk is greatest; (iv) consumer acceptance, which depends on trust and values, not just safety data.

(b) Key value judgements: (i) How much weight to give food security benefits versus ecological uncertainty? (ii) Should intellectual property over gene-edited varieties be regulated to ensure equitable access? (iii) Should the public have a say in deploying a new agricultural technology, even if scientifically safe? (iv) Should the UK align with EU regulations (which treat some gene-edited crops as GMOs) or diverge (as US and Australia have)?

(c) Precautionary principle: The strong form of precaution — no approval until all uncertainty is resolved — is not warranted here; the risk profile does not differ substantially from conventional breeding, and the potential food security benefits are large. A proportionate precaution is appropriate: phased approval with monitoring requirements, mandatory reporting of ecological impacts, and a built-in review at 5 years.

(d) Governance recommendation: Adopt a risk-proportionate regulatory framework that evaluates gene-edited traits by their characteristics, not the editing technique. Require field trials with ecological monitoring before full commercial approval. Establish a mandatory gene-edited crop register for traceability. Conduct a structured public dialogue (not just consultation) before final approval, enabling genuine two-way engagement. Include a 5-year sunset clause for the regulatory approval, triggering automatic review. Commission an independent equity assessment of intellectual property arrangements before patent protection is finalised.

rabbitHoleTerms.description: Stokes's (1997) two-dimensional taxonomy of research: basic versus applied is replaced by quest for fundamental understanding and use-inspiration, identifying use-inspired basic research as a neglected and valuable category.

Gibbons et al.'s concept of research conducted in application contexts, transdisciplinarily, with societal accountability — contrasted with Mode 1 (disciplinary, curiosity-driven, peer-reviewed academic science).

The deliberate production and promotion of scientific doubt about established findings by industries whose products face regulation — documented in tobacco, fossil fuels, pesticides, and pharmaceuticals.

Pielke's role for scientists who answer specific factual questions posed by policymakers without advocating for a policy position — appropriate when the science is clear and the policy question is factual.

Trade-Related Aspects of Intellectual Property Rights — the WTO agreement that standardises intellectual property protection globally, with major implications for access to medicines and agricultural technologies in developing countries.
Science Advice for Policy by European Academies — the EU's current mechanism for providing independent scientific advice, replacing the discontinued Chief Scientific Adviser role.

questions.questionHtml: What is Stokes's 'Pasteur's quadrant' in research classification?
options: Use-inspired basic research — work driven by both quest for fundamental understanding and consideration of practical use, exemplified by Pasteur's germ theory research
Applied research that directly addresses practical problems without generating fundamental theoretical knowledge
Basic research conducted in university settings, funded by government, without regard for practical applications
Translational research that bridges the gap between basic science findings and clinical or industrial applications
questions.correctAnswer: Use-inspired basic research — work driven by both quest for fundamental understanding and consideration of practical use, exemplified by Pasteur's germ theory research
questions.explanationHtml: Stokes's two-dimensional framework places research along two axes: quest for fundamental understanding and use-inspiration. Pasteur's quadrant occupies the high-high position: research simultaneously advancing theoretical knowledge and motivated by practical application. Stokes argues this quadrant is most neglected by science policy frameworks that privilege either pure basic research (Bohr's atom — high understanding, low use) or purely applied research (Edison's lab — low understanding, high use).

questions.questionHtml: During a public health crisis, the government's chief scientific adviser states: 'The models predict that without intervention, 500,000 deaths will occur. The government must implement a national lockdown.' What error is the adviser making, according to Pielke's framework?
options: The adviser is acting as an issue advocate — treating a policy prescription as if it followed directly from scientific evidence, conflating factual and value judgements
The adviser is acting as a science arbiter — appropriately translating model outputs into policy recommendations
The adviser is practicing honest brokering — presenting the evidence-based options to government
The adviser is acting as a pure scientist — correctly communicating uncertainty in model predictions
questions.correctAnswer: The adviser is acting as an issue advocate — treating a policy prescription as if it followed directly from scientific evidence, conflating factual and value judgements
questions.explanationHtml: The model prediction is scientific; the policy prescription ('must implement lockdown') is not uniquely determined by it. Multiple policies are consistent with the modelling: tiered restrictions, voluntary measures, regional variations, lockdowns of different strictness. Each involves value judgements about acceptable mortality risk, economic harm, civil liberties, and distributional equity. By declaring that the science 'demands' a specific policy, the adviser is acting as an issue advocate — using scientific authority to advance a specific policy choice without acknowledging the value judgements involved. The honest broker would present: 'the models project X deaths without intervention; here are four intervention options with their projected mortality and economic costs.'

questions.questionHtml: The tobacco industry funded research in the 1950s–1980s that consistently found no statistically significant link between smoking and cancer at the p < 0.05 threshold. Why is this strategy of 'manufactured uncertainty' so effective even when the scientific consensus clearly supports the causal link?
options: It exploits the fact that statistical significance at p < 0.05 is not equivalent to scientific consensus — individual underpowered studies can fail to reach significance even when the true effect is real and well-established
It works because p < 0.05 studies are always correct and consensus-based research is always biased
It is effective because most scientists are unable to distinguish between well-conducted and poorly-conducted research
It relies on the public's genuine inability to understand probability, which makes any uncertainty claim persuasive regardless of its scientific merit
questions.correctAnswer: It exploits the fact that statistical significance at p < 0.05 is not equivalent to scientific consensus — individual underpowered studies can fail to reach significance even when the true effect is real and well-established
questions.explanationHtml: The manufactured uncertainty strategy is sophisticated: by funding many small, underpowered studies designed to fail to reach p < 0.05 (often by using non-representative samples, short follow-up periods, or poorly measured outcomes), the industry could create a literature of 'negative studies' while the epidemiological consensus (based on cohort studies with millions of participants and decades of follow-up) was overwhelming. This exploits the asymmetry between scientific consensus (accumulated evidence from multiple study designs) and individual study results (which can fail to detect real effects due to insufficient power). It also exploits journalists' tendency to treat individual studies as definitive and to frame scientific consensus as just another opinion.
